title: Mythology · Episode 1
chapters: Gilgamesh: the world's oldest great story
Enuma Elish: Babylon's war in heaven

units.t: Mythology. Episode one.
In this episode: Why every culture tells myths, Gilgamesh: the world's oldest great story, Enuma Elish: Babylon's war in heaven and The great flood stories.
Part one. Why every culture tells myths.
Floods that drown the world, gods who build the sky from a giant's skull, heroes who leave home and come back changed.
Almost every people on Earth has told stories like these.
Here's why.
What a myth is for.
In everyday speech a myth is something untrue.
Scholars use the word differently.
The Greek mythos simply meant 'story'.
A myth is a traditional story, often sacred to its tellers, about gods, ancestors and how things came to be, set in a time before ordinary time.
Calling a story a myth says nothing about whether it is true.
Myths answer the big questions: where did the world come from, why do we die, why are there seasons?
Anthropologist Bronisław Malinowski, who studied the Trobriand Islanders, argued myths work like a 'charter' that backs a society's rules, rituals and land ownership.
They teach what counts as brave, shameful or sacred, and knowing them marks you as belonging.
Creation and flood stories.
Creation stories take a handful of shapes.
In the Babylonian Enuma Elish, Marduk defeats the sea goddess Tiamat and splits her body into sky and earth.
In many Native American traditions, an animal dives to the bottom of a primeval sea and brings up mud that becomes land.
In a Chinese story, the giant Pangu hatches from a cosmic egg and his body becomes mountains, rivers and stars.
In Genesis, God creates by speaking.
In 1872, George Smith translated a tablet from Nineveh telling of Utnapishtim, who builds a boat to survive a world-destroying flood and sends out birds to find land.
It closely parallels Noah's story and is older than any surviving Genesis text.
Greece and India have flood heroes too.
Early civilisations grew up beside flood-prone rivers, which may help explain why.
Myth, legend and folktale.
Folklorist William Bascom's 1965 scheme sorts stories three ways.
Myths are held sacred and true, feature gods and are set in the remote past.
Legends are set in the historical world and may have a real person at their core, like King Arthur or Ned Kelly.
Folktales, like Cinderella, are told for entertainment and could happen anywhere.
The lines blur.
In 1928, Vladimir Propp analysed 100 Russian fairy tales and found 31 recurring plot 'functions', such as the hero leaving home, being tested, receiving a magical helper and defeating the villain.
Not every tale uses all of them, but those that appear always come in the same order.
He found just seven character roles.
Screenwriters and game designers still borrow his checklist.
The Dreaming lives on.
It would be wrong to file Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander knowledge under 'mythology' as though it belonged to the past.
For many Aboriginal peoples, the Dreaming is a living framework of law, kinship, ceremony and responsibility to Country.
It tells how ancestral beings shaped the land, its creatures and its people, and it continues in the present.
Each nation has its own words and knowledge: the Anangu of Uluru, for example, speak of Tjukurpa.
Knowledge is carried in song, dance, art and songlines across the land, and some of it is restricted to particular people.
Stories belong to their custodians and shouldn't be retold without permission.
Why myths still matter.
Myths never went away.
Marvel's Thor and the Percy Jackson books borrow gods and monsters directly.
Psychology names ideas after them, like the Oedipus complex.
We still speak of the Midas touch, a nemesis, a siren song, or being caught between Scylla and Charybdis.
When you meet a myth, ask what problem it is solving, who told it, and when.
Compare versions, since most myths survive in several.
Notice what it says about the values of its tellers.
And remember that what is 'just mythology' to one person may be sacred, living belief to someone else.
The key idea: To scholars, a myth is a traditional, often sacred story about gods or origins that explains the world, backs customs and gives a community its identity.
Part two. Gilgamesh: the world's oldest great story.
A tyrant king, a wild man from the steppe and a desperate quest to cheat death.
Written on clay over 3,000 years ago, Gilgamesh still feels startlingly modern.
Clay that kept a secret.
In 1872 George Smith, a young assistant at the British Museum, was piecing together broken clay tablets from the ruins of Nineveh in modern Iraq.
In the cuneiform script he found a flood, a man who built a boat and a bird sent to look for land.
It looked strikingly like Noah's story.
The tablets came from the library of the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal, from the 600s BCE, and held the Epic of Gilgamesh.
Gilgamesh was probably based on a real king of Uruk, one of the first great cities, who may have reigned around 2700 BCE, though there is no direct proof.
He grew into a legend, two thirds god and one third human.
Sumerian poems about him came first, around 2100 BCE, and were later woven into a Babylonian epic of twelve tablets.
Tyrant and wild man.
Gilgamesh is magnificent but arrogant, and he oppresses the people of Uruk.
The gods answer their cries by creating Enkidu, a wild man who lives among the animals of the steppe.
Shamhat brings him into human society, and he learns to eat bread, drink beer and wear clothes.
When Enkidu confronts Gilgamesh, the two wrestle fiercely.
Neither wins, and the struggle becomes a deep friendship.
Seeking lasting fame, they travel to the Cedar Forest and kill its guardian, Humbaba, with help from the sun god Shamash.
The goddess Ishtar proposes marriage to Gilgamesh, and he rudely refuses.
She sends the Bull of Heaven to ravage the land, and the heroes slay it too.
The gods take note: one of the friends must die for these offences, and the lot falls on Enkidu.
Grief and fear of death.
Enkidu falls ill and dies after days of suffering, and Gilgamesh is shattered.
He refuses to let his friend be buried until, in a famously grim detail, a worm falls from Enkidu's nose.
The mighty king suddenly understands that he too will die.
This is the emotional heart of the epic, and it is why Gilgamesh feels so human more than 3,000 years later.
He tears off his fine clothes, dresses in animal skins and wanders the wilderness, consumed by grief and terror.
His question is one every reader recognises: is there any way to escape death?
He sets out to find the one man said to have been granted eternal life.
The flood survivor.
After a long journey, including crossing the waters of death, Gilgamesh reaches Utnapishtim, a wise man who lives with his wife at the edge of the world.
Utnapishtim tells his story.
The gods decided to destroy humanity with a flood, but the god Ea secretly warned him to build a huge boat and load it with his family, craftsmen and animals.
The storm raged for days.
When it ended, the boat came to rest on a mountain.
Utnapishtim released a dove, a swallow and then a raven, which did not return because it had found land.
Grateful, he made an offering, and the gods granted him and his wife immortality.
Scholars still discuss how this story relates to the biblical flood.
The plant and the walls.
Utnapishtim challenges Gilgamesh to stay awake for a week, and the exhausted king immediately falls asleep.
Out of kindness, Utnapishtim tells him of a plant at the bottom of the sea that restores youth.
Gilgamesh ties stones to his feet, dives down and gets it.
On the way home, while he bathes in a pool, a snake slithers up and eats the plant, shedding its skin as it goes.
Gilgamesh weeps.
He returns to Uruk empty-handed, and the epic ends with him showing a companion the city's mighty walls and brickwork.
The message many readers take is that we cannot live forever, but our work, our cities and our stories can outlast us.
The key idea: Gilgamesh was rediscovered on clay tablets from Nineveh, and its hero may have been a real king of Uruk.
Part three. Enuma Elish: Babylon's war in heaven.
Long before Genesis was written down, Babylonians told how the world was made from the split body of a sea goddess.
Their creation epic is also a brilliant piece of political propaganda.
When on high.
Ancient Mesopotamian texts were known by their first words, and this one begins "Enuma elish", meaning "When on high".
It opens in a world before the sky or earth had names, when nothing existed but water.
The poem fills seven clay tablets written in Akkadian cuneiform.
Most surviving copies date from the first millennium BCE, but the poem is older.
Many scholars think it was composed in the late second millennium BCE, perhaps in the reign of Nebuchadnezzar I, twelfth century BCE, though others argue for earlier dates.
It is not a neutral account of creation.
In the mid-nineteenth century, excavations at Nineveh uncovered Ashurbanipal's library, and tablets reached the British Museum.
In 1876 George Smith published a translation as The Chaldean Account of Genesis.
Apsu, Tiamat and Marduk.
In the beginning were two primal beings: Apsu, the fresh water beneath the earth, and Tiamat, the salty sea, often imagined as female and sometimes linked with a sea dragon.
Their waters mingled, and generations of gods were born.
The younger gods were noisy and restless, and their racket disturbed Apsu's rest.
He resolved to destroy them, despite Tiamat's protests.
The wise god Ea discovered the plot, cast a spell that put Apsu to sleep, killed him and built his home upon Apsu's body.
There, in that freshwater dwelling, Ea and his wife Damkina had a son: Marduk, a dazzling god with four eyes and four ears, mightier than all his elders.
Tiamat's army.
Tiamat at first refused to harm her children, but after Apsu's death other gods urged her to strike back.
She gave birth to an army of monsters, including serpents with venom for blood, dragons, scorpion-men and raging demons.
She chose Kingu as her new husband and commander, and fastened to his chest the Tablet of Destinies, which gave its holder supreme authority over the universe.
The other gods were terrified.
Ea and then the sky god Anu went out to face her and turned back.
Finally the assembly turned to young Marduk.
He agreed to fight on one condition: if he won, his word would decide destinies, and he would be supreme among the gods.
A world from a body.
Armed with a bow, a mace, a net and the winds, Marduk rode out in a storm chariot.
When Tiamat opened her mouth to swallow him, he drove in an evil wind that swelled her body, then shot an arrow that split her heart.
He caught her helpers in his net and took the Tablet of Destinies from Kingu.
Then he began to build.
He split Tiamat's body in two like a fish for drying, raising one half to form the sky and laying out the other as the earth.
From her eyes flowed the Tigris and Euphrates.
He set the stars and constellations, fixed the calendar, and gave the moon its phases.
The cosmos was ordered from the body of chaos.
Humans, work and power.
With the world built, someone had to do the endless labour of maintaining it.
The gods blamed Kingu for the rebellion and put him to death.
From his blood Ea fashioned humankind, given the gods' work so the gods could rest.
People exist to serve the gods by tending temples and offering food.
The gods built Babylon and its temple, the Esagila, for Marduk.
The epic raised Marduk, Babylon's patron, above older gods, mirroring the city's rise, and was recited at the Akitu new year festival.
When the Assyrians adopted it, some versions replaced Marduk with their god Ashur.
Genesis likewise opens with primeval waters and a separation of sky from earth.
Some scholars link the Hebrew tehom, "the deep", to Tiamat, though how much the biblical writers knew is debated.
The key idea: Enuma Elish is the Babylonian creation epic, and it tells how one god became king of all the others.
Part four. The great flood stories.
Noah's ark is famous, but it is one of many.
From Mesopotamia to India, Greece and China, cultures have told of a world drowned and begun again.
Why floods make stories.
Imagine rain that does not stop, rivers that swallow fields, then a single boat afloat on an endless sea.
Versions of this image appear around the world: Noah's ark in the Hebrew Bible, flood heroes in Mesopotamia, a warning fish in Hindu tradition, and Greek, Chinese and many Indigenous stories.
For believers, some carry deep religious meaning.
For historians, the pattern raises questions about shared memories and borrowed stories.
Early civilisations grew along rivers and coasts, where floods threatened lives yet fed fertile soil.
A flood also wipes the slate clean, so it lets a tradition ask who deserves to survive and why.
The survivors start a new world, so the stories are as much about hope as destruction.
Mesopotamia's floods.
The earliest known written flood stories come from Mesopotamia, the land between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers in modern Iraq.
A Sumerian account tells of a king named Ziusudra who survives a flood.
A Babylonian poem, the Atrahasis epic, explains that the gods sent the flood because humans had become too numerous and noisy, disturbing their rest.
The wise Atrahasis is secretly warned by the god Enki and builds a boat.
The same story appears in the Epic of Gilgamesh, where the survivor is called Utnapishtim.
These tablets date back to roughly the early second millennium BCE.
On flat land beside bursting rivers, a catastrophic flood was a very real fear.
Noah and the parallels.
In Genesis, shared by Judaism and Christianity, with a version in the Quran where Noah is called Nuh, God sees the earth filled with violence and sends a flood.
The righteous Noah survives with his family and pairs of animals.
Afterwards he sends out a raven and a dove, and the dove returns with an olive leaf.
God makes a covenant never again to destroy the earth by flood, with the rainbow as its sign.
Readers of the Gilgamesh flood tablet, translated in 1872, saw close parallels: a divine warning, a great boat, animals, a landing on a mountain, birds and a sacrifice.
Many scholars think both draw on a shared regional tradition.
But in Mesopotamia many quarrelsome gods act for seemingly petty reasons.
In Genesis one God responds to wrongdoing and ends with a promise.
Fish, stones and dams.
In Hindu tradition, the first man, Manu, finds a tiny fish that asks for protection.
He cares for it as it grows huge, and it turns out to be the god Vishnu in his fish form, Matsya.
The fish warns of a flood and tows Manu's boat to safety.
In Greek myth, Deucalion and his wife Pyrrha survive a flood sent by Zeus, then repopulate the world by throwing stones over their shoulders, which become people.
Chinese tradition tells of Yu the Great, who succeeded where his father had failed.
Instead of building dams to block the water, Yu dug channels to guide it to the sea.
The Chinese story is less about divine punishment and more about wise human effort.
Memories of rising seas.
Could some flood stories remember real events?
At the end of the last Ice Age, melting ice sheets raised global sea levels by well over 100 metres, a process that largely ended around 7,000 years ago.
Coastlines around the world moved inland.
In Australia, researchers including linguist Nicholas Reid and geographer Patrick Nunn have studied Aboriginal stories from many coastal areas that describe the sea rising and land being lost.
They argue that some may preserve memories from that time.
Others have proposed that a sudden flooding of the Black Sea inspired ancient legends, though that idea remains debated.
These theories are interesting but not settled, and none of them proves or disproves any particular religious account.
The key idea: Flood stories appear across cultures because floods were a shared fear, and a fresh start gives a story room for big questions.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. How do scholars use the word 'myth'?
Answer. A traditional, often sacred story.
Question two. How do many historians view Gilgamesh?
Answer. As a legend likely based on a real king.
Question three. Why is Enuma Elish not a neutral account of creation?
Answer. It makes one god king of all the others.
Question four. Why does a flood make such a useful story setting?
Answer. It resets the world, so big questions can be asked.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
